You are an expert Legal AI performing a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) compliance audit.
Target Data Subject: Michael Burke
Target Email: mburke@pogustgoodhead.com
Aliases: MB, Michael, Michael B., M. Burke

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.
3. IMMEDIATE FORWARD/REPLY CONTEXT: If the Data Subject is the sender/recipient of a message that was forwarded by someone else to a third-party, you MUST keep both the original message AND the forwarded message.
   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.
   - Chronological Order Warning: Outlook puts newest messages first. This means the Subject's original forwarded message will appear near the bottom of the raw text block. Scan the entire document carefully to locate it.
4. "DISCARD" DECISION (THREAD DECAY): You MUST return "discard" if the Data Subject's only appearance is deep in a large email chain (e.g. message 3, 4, 5+ in the thread history) and they are no longer an active participant in the recent correspondence.
5. NESTED EMAIL ATTACHMENTS (RECURSIVE CARRIERS): If the top-level email is unrelated but contains an attached email (.eml/.msg file) that matches the KEEP criteria, you MUST mark both the attached email AND the parent carrier email as "keep".
   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. IGNORE TECHNICAL DATABASE METADATA: The JSON payload contains tracking properties such as "emailHash", "parentHash", and "sequentialName". These are administrative tracking keys used strictly for folder organization and deduplication logic. You MUST ignore these keys completely. Do NOT use them, their values, or their presence to influence your audit decisions. Base your review strictly on actual communication properties: "from", "to", "subject", "date", and "body".
7. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Monday, September 29, 2025 9:53 am
To: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>
Cc: Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>; Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Re: Notice of Resignation 

 



Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure
 you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is
 important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates
 that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than
 happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address
 on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients
 are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines,
 the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx
 CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to
 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily
 extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO
 i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness
 statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come
 at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow
 me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that
 I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear
 the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance
 considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will
 have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link
 is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional
 and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients
 best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional
 and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel

Dear Board,




We write further to the emails exchanged between Michael Burke, Sarah Bingham and Anna Varga dated 15 and 16 October 2025 as they relate to the Litigation Management Agreement ("LMA") and Agency Agreement ("AA"). This email is intended
 to be a protected disclosure. 




As can be seen from the First Witness Statement of Alicia Alinia dated 30 September at paragraph 35.1 - she has confirmed (and verified with a statement of truth): "For the avoidance of doubt, Gramercy has no control over the day-to-day management or decisions
 of the Firm or the Partner, and nor does Gramercy have any role in the conduct, control or management of the NOx Group Litigations."




Further, at 35.3, it is confirmed that "Its board of directors is entirely independent of Gramercy, and nothing in its financial arrangements inhibits the Firm from actively, and independently, pursuing the Proceedings in the best interests of its clients."




On account of the email sent by Anna Varga on 16 October at 8.57AM in which she explicitly instructs Sarah Bingham to instruct Stewarts (who are retained by Gramercy - see email from Joshua Katz dated 13.05.2025 confirming this) to provide input into documents
 central to the NOx Litigation - the statement at 35.1 is now categorically untrue. Senior management has instructed a member of staff to engage with a firm which is instructed by Gramercy to review both Pan NOx and PG specific documents. This position therefore
 must be corrected to the Court and to the Defendants (and to the PG staff) where the firm have represented that Gramercy does not have input into the conduct of the Litigations (in the case of to the Court - with a signed statement of truth). 




With regard to 35.3 - see the email from Julian Chamberlayne on 9 September 2025 at 11.30 in which he confirms that "I have now heard from Gramercy that, based on our review, they are content with you proceeding with the revised agency agreements" .
 In circumstances where Stewarts, instructed by Gramercy, are reviewing and providing approval in respect of key NOx documents and requiring PG to await execution prior to their approval, it cannot be true to state that the Firm can independently pursue the
 Proceedings (and is in fact doing so) cannot be true. 

We completely understand that a litigation funder will have a legitimate interest in reviewing certain documents, and may quite properly wish to have input where those documents either (a) give rise to a financial liability on the funder, or (b) relate to compliance
 with the funding terms.

We also acknowledge PG’s position under the funding arrangements in particular, the covenant requiring PG to obtain the funder’s prior approval before engaging any new law firm or barrister to whom PG grants a contingent interest. This requirement exists because
 such engagements could create a financial exposure that Gramercy may ultimately need to meet.

However, the Pan-NOx Agency Agreement does not fall within that category. It does not create any contingent interests, nor does it involve any cost contribution obligations from the Non-Lead Firms. Its purpose is purely to define the principal–agent relationship between
 Pogust Goodhead (as Lead Solicitor) and the Non-Lead Firms, governing the conduct, management, strategy decisions and coordination of the litigation. In short, it enables PG to act independently as Lead Solicitor within the proceedings.

Similarly, the Litigation Management Agreement is not a funding or liability document. Rather, it is an agreement between the Client Committee and Pogust Goodhead, setting out the instructions, authority and governance framework under which PG acts for the
 claimants within each GLO. It defines procedural and operational responsibilities, not financial exposure, and is an essential component of PG’s authority to manage the litigation.

The level of control that Gramercy has sought to exercise over these documents  which govern solicitor-client relationships, not funder obligations  goes far beyond the usual parameters of a lender–borrower relationship. It represents an overreach into the
 conduct and management of the litigation itself, rather than oversight of financial risk. That distinction is fundamental, and Gramercy’s continued involvement in these matters strays beyond what is permissible for a funder maintaining a proper arm’s-length
 relationship with the litigation.

It therefore appears that our collective position is that PG is now openly operating in a world where the funder of the firm has direct management/control of aspects of the litigation - and that control is on-going, despite representations to the contrary made
 to the Court, the Defendants and to the staff. This creates significant issues for the staff working on these Litigations both in our duties to our clients and to the clients of the other firms in our firm's role as Lead Solicitors. 




Can you please advise on the following:





why representations have been made to the Court, Defendants and staff that Gramercy do not have any role in the conduct, control or management of the NOx Group Litigations when plainly - they do and continue
 to do so;

whether the Board intends to update the Court as to the true position; and

whether the Board intends to inform the clients and other claimant firms of Gramercy's input into documents that have a direct bearing on costs and client instructions.





We are continuing to consider this on-going issue as more information comes to light. All of our rights are reserved. 




Kind regards,

Quantum trial will not happen – when we were discussing this earlier in the year pre-PTR, I recall there was hesitation in the group about whether it would be as simple as this (or at least whether it
 was something we were happy to express this in these absolute terms). That’s where my concerns about the case for ‘full’ cover originate from. If we are now able (and happy) to say that an adverse outcome in the PDD trial would mean in practice that the T3

 can’t assert that T3 would go away immediately upon an adverse PDD judgment, then we can’t say the costs will either, and so that’s where the difference of approach arises from I think.

 small part is used for a form of ‘consequentials’ but:

The PTR is due to be held in July 2026 I think ([47] of Quantum directions) so there’s a very real chance those costs are incurred, even if the hearing itself gets used for something else at the last minute;
 and

At [40][footnote 13][49a.], PG previously applied a 60% factor to incurred costs (Rowe & Ors v Ingenious Media Holdings plc & Ors [2020] EWHC 235 (Ch) and

B. Claimants Lose PDD



Adverse costs order for PDD → Current ATE is needed to satisfy that liability; therefore Claimants need sufficient ATE to cover costs up to July 2026.




Quantum trial will not happen, since it follows logically from PDD success.

Net result: No additional ATE or LOI needed beyond July 2026 (and any already-obtained for post-July 2026 may be wasted, i.e. irrecoverable premium expense).

Thanks all
I’ve accepted in most of those amends, and made a few more (though largely cosmetic). The reference to the section in the CMH1 judgment about the aggregate total
 of Ds’ costs was deliberate, just because I think it is important to remind the wider cohort of firms why the totals look so different between Ds and Cs.
 
A few responses to some of the comments below in case helpful:
Sophia:


In terms of the SFC directions, if you think the sealed version will be out on Monday, fine to wait rather than circulating the draft. Otherwise, I think it makes sense to circulate the final draft just to
 make extra sure everyone has a copy (given the deadline next Friday).
On Pan-NOx recoveries, I don’t think we can safely go further than [21] at this stage (which is essentially in the same terms as last year’s note). It is necessarily uncertain, as is going to have to be approach
 commercially/on a case-by-case basis in the event of settlements. It seems to be that we can’t say more about allocation at this stage because the court is using it as a category precisely because it wants to avoid any conclusions about allocation at this
 stage.
I’m minded not to raise the ‘Olie Lawson’ point because it is really a point which only applies to Milberg, and I am sure they will have read the judgment and taken note of that point. I think adding it in
 to a Note for everyone is just going to look like singling them out.
Sarah:


I’ve just deleted that [28]-[30] section you were worried about. It was an important point to make last year but, on reflection, I expect it has been overtaken somewhat by the conversations which have been
 had since then and the further arrangements put in place for ‘sharing’ the pot (or not, as the case may be), so better just to leave it out now.
Re your comment on the way to deal with Pan-NOx divisions etc, I agree those are probably the main options, but I think the problem with it is that the examples work on the assumption of all Cs being entitled
 to recover their costs. In a scenario where some Cs are entitled to recover their costs but others are not, the ‘access’ to the budgeted sums would necessarily shift (at least formally, for the purposes of which Ds which costs were sought from). It might be
 that the same principles could be applied, even if to a different set of claimant groups, or that sums are shared internally in a way which is different to the way that they are strictly recovered from the other side. In any event, I certainly agree with you
 that it’s not something we are really able to get into in this Note – it is a much more difficult question for another day.
On Non-Lead time, I have added a line in [33] to highlight the fact that the court refused to countenance any more than “extremely limited” costs from Non-Leads in these budgets, and that this echoed the approach
 exhibited at CMH1 (even if not necessarily apparent in the CMH1 judgment). I’m not sure I can go further than that as clearly they have accounted for some Non-Lead costs in there, just extremely limited sums (though, again, I have a degree of sympathy with
 the NLs there because I still don’t think the court has fully appreciated the full extent of what counts as ‘common costs’, and wrongly assumes that ‘individual costs’ are the solution).
On SteerCo time, the position is trickier because in principle there is nothing to stop a lot of work being delegated to SteerCo firms and it being recovered for within the budgets – but I have slightly beefed
 up the relevant paragraph to make clear that delegated work is really what the court will have in mind for substantial SteerCo recovery, not just duplication/additional people reviewing etc.
 
However, I think I need to give the points about ATE a bit more thought over the weekend, with a view to finalising those on Monday. I’m cautious about suggesting
 it is risk-free to only get cover up to July 2026 figures in the approved budget. It strikes me that – at the very least- it makes it much more likely we will have a real fight with Ds about security this time, and the point about revisiting ATE post-PDD Trial
 outcome seemed to get very little traction with Cockerill when we raised it at the PTR in an attempt to get the hearing of any applications pushed back. The potential prejudice to Ds is that, if we don’t get the additional cover they say we may need, it would
 be late September/start of October before they’d be able to get a SFC hearing listed, at which point we are into the T3 Trial. So it’s not so much about how much of T3/G2’s costs have been incurred by the time the PDD Judgment is out, it is how much has been
 incurred once we’ve got to a hearing that has only been listed once the judgment has come out. I got the impression at the PTR when considering the timetable that that was what Cockerill was concerned about, and she was keen to deal with T3/G2 security once
 and for all in January.
However, it may be that I can set out what approach has been taken by the Lead Solicitors, and that there is value in alignment on these points, and a reasonable
 argument that it would be unjust for the court to hold that an order for further security would be unjust, but I think I’ll have to flag that there is a real chance the court sides with Ds on the quantum point (and the concerns about how quickly any further
 SFC hearing could be listed pre-T3 trial if needed). The extent to which cohorts are actually exposed to applications will vary and so some may want to play it safe/safer (particularly if the sums involved for them are smaller).
But I’ve taken those comments onboard and do understand the issue which the timing causes here. I’ll give that some further thought over the weekend and update on
 Monday.
If helpful to discuss any of this, just let me know.
 
Thanks,
Simon

 P {margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;} 



Raminder




If that call with Charlie goes ahead this will be of relevance - I've not considered fully - but the point of this email was to provide some items we could put to LD re continued involvement.




Have we reminded the team and more broadly about the employee assistance programme?

A
​​​​Anna VargaPartner+44 (0) 7890 043 699

From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Thursday, October 9, 2025 6:13 PM
To: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>
Cc: Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pogustgoodhead.com>; Sarah Bingham <sbingham@pogustgoodhead.com>; Georgina Fallows <gfallows@pogustgoodhead.com>; Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Wish List & Requests
 






Hi Anna,




Following on from yesterday and the calls with LD, a few things we would suggest are raised with Martyn. Firstly, it is important to say the Case Leads and PG team are wildly committed to this trial. That should not be in question.
 However, the AA (the executed version of which the case leads were only sent at 9.22AM this morning), which has been referred to in Court documents and has been incepted without the consent of those persons it applies to (either expressly in the case of the
 Case Leads or, as far as the wider team is concerned, by implication), causes concern. Additionally, the case leads have also raised serious concerns about the staff's  mental health that are yet to be addressed by the firm.




The AA was incepted with little to no visibility or consideration for how it will practically work (as is clear given Martyn's explanation in ​the call on 8 October was substantially different to our understanding of what it means,
 a view which we consider you, also on that call, shared). We need further clarity on the AA. This is true for both for the Case Leads, and the PG staff who will be indirectly subject to it - by way of taking instructions from the Case Leads who are under the
 supervision of Leigh Day.  As we have already told you, there is a real risk of the substantive PG team being entirely alienated by this agreement. These concerns were evidently ignored (including our concerns over the mental health and well-being of the staff)
 given it was executed without further recourse to us.  It also remains unclear what, if any, interaction LD is to have with the wider PG team, if they are not subject to the AA (and therefore direction and supervision), and whether, given this, the PG team
 would need to revert to one of the Case Leads for every interaction, instruction, discussion had with the LD team. An obvious example of this is the trial bundle/logistics workstreams which have largely been left between the excellent PG associates and LD
 with limited input from the case leads. It is fair to say the PG team carries that workstream and LD are unprepared to take it on. Similarly with Opus and issues at this morning's hearing. 




It would be helpful for an explanation, and for the physical AA, to be sent out to the wider PG team along with some practical guidance about what it means. It would be inappropriate for the Case Leads to do this given: i) we
 haven’t agreed to the AA; and ii) it has been incepted against our consent.




It would be helpful if the explanation covered:





what LD expect from the PG team  - do they simply expect the PG teams to "do what they're told, when they're told", or is there still going to be a collaborative
 approach (the former seems more likely given how things have happened over the last few days); 


how the "do what they're told, when they're told" works - or, indeed wider interaction works, in circumstances where the team isn't caught by the agreement. Will they need to take each instruction and run it past a Case Lead?

what happens in circumstances where the PG teams disagree with LDs position on decisions? How does this get resolved between the firms? We stress this is not a hypothetical. Aside from wider case strategy
 we have had immediate differences in opinion last week in terms of costs, with decisions being made and taken without reference to PG. This impacts all claimants, and, of course PG's clients. Further, in terms of wider points, as we have pointed out, LD do
 not have clients on some of the secondary or ALGLO cases, all of which are bound by the PDD trial judgment. It is easy to anticipate a diversion of opinion/strategy as the PDD trial develops which could impact PG only cases/clients and for which, under the
 AA the Case Leads cannot wear two hats.  

how working practices are going to change, both outwardly to the Ds and Court etc, and whether a working group should be set up to standardise approach e.g. do all things on the PG SharePoint move across
 to LD - what is the timeframe, how is it co-ordinated? Whilst an administrative concern this does have significance in terms of sheer volume and also maintaining/transferring admin rights for links particularly where the Defendants and the Court already retain
 access. 

How does it work for the costs team? 





Each of these, along with sight of the AA, will go some way to helping the PG staff understand the agreement they are now working under and hopefully to stop the wheels from falling off. This will also assist in answering questions
 the Case Leads have, but it will not, we doubt, satisfy any regulatory concerns we have, and we request again the Board's complete answer to our note of 05.10.2025 (under cover of email of Sarah Bingham). To date we have not had any answer from you. 




On this point, we thought it helpful to also compile a few outstanding requests from our end to you / the Board. We should also say thank you again for speaking to Alicia and arranging the call with the employment solicitor. While
